holidays.name: National Welsh Rarebit Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate cheesy, saucy toast. Welsh rarebit is a rich, tangy sauce of melted cheese, mustard, Worcestershire sauce and often beer, poured over toast and broiled until bubbly. Pour a pint, grab a fork and get gooey.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance with no clear founder. The dish itself dates back to 18th-century Britain.
holidays.funFact: There is no rabbit in Welsh rarebit. The name was probably a cheeky joke that the Welsh were so poor, cheese on toast was the best they could get instead of meat.

holidays.name: National Skyscraper Day
holidays.description: A day to look up and admire the towering buildings that scrape the clouds. Tilt your head back and appreciate the steel, glass and ambition behind the world's tallest structures.
holidays.origin: It is celebrated on the birthday of architect Louis Sullivan, born September 3, 1856. He is often called the father of skyscrapers and the mentor of Frank Lloyd Wright.
holidays.funFact: Sullivan's maxim that form ever follows function became one of the most famous principles in modern architecture.

holidays.name: Penny Press Day
holidays.description: A salute to the cheap, punchy newspapers that put the news in everyone's hands for a single cent. Penny papers were packed with crime stories, gossip and human-interest tales, and they changed how people read the news.
holidays.origin: It commemorates September 3, 1833, when Benjamin Day launched The New York Sun, the first successful penny newspaper in the United States.
holidays.funFact: The Sun sold for just one cent, while rival papers cost about six cents. Newsboys hawking it on street corners helped popularize the newspaper-selling trade.
